# `•decompose` — Matrix decompositions

`kind •decompose m` factors the matrix `m` and returns the factors as a record. `kind` names the decomposition, as text or as the `kind` of a record of options:

| `kind` | Fields | Factors |
|---|---|---|
| `"svd"` | `u`, `s`, `v` | `m` is `u×⍤1s +.× +⍉v`, with the singular values `s` in descending order |
| `"qr"` | `q`, `r` | `m` is `q+.×r`, with orthonormal columns in `q`, and `r` upper triangular |
| `"eigen"` | `values`, `vectors` | each column of `vectors` is an eigenvector of `m`, for the eigenvalue at the same position in `values` |
| `"cholesky"` | `l` | `m` is `l+.×+⍉l`, with `l` lower triangular |
| `"lu"` | `l`, `u`, `p` | `[p]⌷m` is `l+.×u`, with `l` lower triangular with 1 on its diagonal, `u` upper triangular, and `p` the rows' positions |

The SVD and the QR decomposition are thin, unless option `complete` asks for the complete QR. For an `r`-by-`c` matrix, `u` and `q` have `r⌊c` columns. The factors are floats, apart from `"lu"`'s positions `p`. A real matrix gives real factors, apart from complex eigenvalues and their eigenvectors. A Hermitian matrix, one equal to its conjugate transpose, has real eigenvalues in ascending order and orthonormal eigenvectors. Each eigenvector of a real matrix has unit length. [`⌹`](../glyphs/domino.qmd) solves linear systems.

```bpl
("svd" •decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s     ⍝ 9.525518091565104 0.5143005806586441
("eigen" •decompose [2 1⋄1 2]).values  ⍝ [1 3]
```

Where option `vectors` is false, `"svd"` and `"eigen"` give only `s` or `values`, in less time. It's true by default. Where option `complete` is true, `"qr"` gives a square `q`, and an `r` with as many rows as `m`. It's false by default.

```bpl
(["kind":"svd" "vectors":$f]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s   ⍝ 9.525518091565104 0.5143005806586441
⍴(["kind":"qr" "complete":$t]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).q  ⍝ [3 3]ₓ
```

Option `rank`, a positive whole number, makes `"svd"` give only the first `rank` singular values, with their vectors unless `vectors` is false. A randomized method computes them, in far less time than the full SVD of a large matrix takes. The result is an approximation. The faster the singular values beyond the `rank`th decay, the smaller its error. For a `rank` within 10 of the matrix's smaller side, the result is the full SVD's first `rank` columns.

```bpl
(["kind":"svd" "rank":1]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).s   ⍝ [9.525518091565104]
⍴(["kind":"svd" "rank":1]•decompose [1 2⋄3 4⋄5 6]).v  ⍝ [2 1]ₓ
```

The determinant is `-.×m`. The `"lu"` factors give its sign, and the logarithm of its magnitude, which can't overflow:

```bpl
f←"lu" •decompose [1 2⋄3 4]
f.p                       ⍝ [1 0]ₓ
d←0 0⍉f.u
-.×f.p=⊗⍳≢f.p × ×/×d     ⍝ ¯1ₓ
+/⍟|d                     ⍝ 0.6931471805599453
```

`kind •decompose⁻¹ factors` multiplies a record of factors back into the matrix, as the table shows. For `"eigen"`, the matrix is `vectors×⍤1values +.× ⌹vectors`, and for `"lu"` it's `[⍋p]⌷l+.×u`. Eigenvectors that aren't independent, such as those of the defective matrix `[1 1⋄0 1]`, can't determine the matrix.

```bpl
f←"cholesky" •decompose [4 2⋄2 3]
"cholesky" •decompose⁻¹ f   ⍝ [4 2⋄2 3]
```

Errors: `RANK` for an argument that isn't a matrix, or a factor of the wrong rank; `LENGTH` for `"eigen"`, `"cholesky"` or `"lu"` of a matrix that isn't square, or factors whose sizes don't agree; `DOMAIN` for an unknown decomposition or option, a `vectors` of false for a kind other than `"svd"` and `"eigen"`, a `complete` of true for a kind other than `"qr"`, a `rank` that isn't a positive whole number or that's given for a kind other than `"svd"`, an empty or nonnumeric matrix, `"cholesky"` of a matrix that isn't Hermitian positive definite, a missing factor, eigenvectors that aren't independent, or a `p` that doesn't hold each position once.
